title: Pediatric Fixed Dilated Pupil & Posterior Synechiae
summary: A comprehensive clinical framework for managing children presenting with pupillary immobility and iridocrystalline adhesions. This guide integrates diagnostic workups for uveitis and trauma with advanced surgical and pharmacological management protocols.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A 'fixed dilated pupil with posterior synechiae (PS)' in a child is a complex clinical scenario where the iris is adhered to the anterior lens capsule in a mid-dilated or dilated state. Unlike the typical miotic pupil of acute uveitis, this presentation often suggests chronic inflammation that was either treated with long-acting cycloplegics (Atropine) during the fibrin-exudative phase or is secondary to blunt trauma with sphincter tear and subsequent inflammation. It carries a high risk of pupillary block glaucoma and amblyopia.

rows: Highest predictor of uveitis risk in JIA (1:160+ titer)
Evaluates for hilar lymphadenopathy or Blau Syndrome
Required if the view is obscured by cataract or PS
Tono-Pen or Icare essential in non-compliant children

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Band Keratopathy**: Calcium deposits at 3 and 9 o'clock in chronic JIA.
**Posterior Synechiae**: 360° adhesion leads to 'Seclusion Pupillae'.
**Iris Bombé**: Forward bowing of iris due to aqueous entrapment.
**Koeppe/Busacca Nodules**: Suggest granulomatous etiology (Sarcoid).
**Complicated Cataract**: Polychromatic luster at the posterior pole.
**Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)**: Most common cause of vision loss.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Pediatric Emergency Signs
content: Sudden ocular pain + nausea (Acute Pupillary Block)
Corneal epithelial edema (High IOP)
Total Seclusion Pupillae (360-degree PS)
Hypopyon (Behcet's or HLA-B27 associated)
White reflex (Leukocoria) in a young child
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) in trauma

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Intensive Topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).
Step 2: Aggressive Mydriasis (Atropine 1% or Phenylephrine 10% to break PS).
Step 3: IOP Control (Aqueous suppressants: Timolol 0.5% or Dorzolamide).
Step 4: Oral Corticosteroids (1mg/kg/day) for severe bilateral cases.
Step 5: Immunomodulatory Therapy (MTX or Adalimumab) for steroid-sparing.

content.explanation: B: Biologics (Adalimumab); R: Refraction (prevent amblyopia); E: Examination under anesthesia (EUA); A: Atropine (break synechiae); K: Keratopathy check (Calcium).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: Synechiolysis
content: Step 1: Paracentesis and injection of Cohesive OVD.
Step 2: Viscosynechiolysis (using OVD to hydraulically separate iris).
Step 3: Mechanical synechiolysis with cyclodialysis spatula.
Step 4: Peripheral Iridectomy (LPI or Surgical) to prevent recurrence.
Step 5: Pupil expansion devices (Malyugin ring) if phaco is required.

sections.title: Surgical Complications & Prognosis
content: Fibrinous Membrane formation (higher in kids).
Secondary Glaucoma (15-30% of chronic cases).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) post-op.
Phthisis Bulbi in end-stage JIA-Uveitis.
Prognosis is generally GOOD if quiescence is achieved for 3 months pre-op.

rows: Adalimumab + MTX is superior to MTX alone in JIA-Uveitis
Standard of care for refractory JIA-uveitis
Long-term safety of MTX, Mycophenolate, and Azathioprine
Validation of safety for steroid-sparing agents
Universal grading for AC cells and flare

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never dilate a child with 360° PS (Seclusion) without a patent peripheral iridectomy; it can trigger acute pupillary block.
The 'Quiet Eye' Rule: Ensure zero AC cells for at least 3 months before elective intraocular surgery.
Traumatic mydriasis without PS often requires only observation or pupillary cerclage later; PS indicates an inflammatory overlay.
In JIA, the eye is often WHITE and PAINLESS despite severe inflammation—regular screening is mandatory.
Phenylephrine 10% should be used with caution in infants due to systemic hypertensive risks.
